question.text:
In the proof of $ eg(p \vee( eg p \wedge q)) \equiv eg p \wedge eg q$, which law justifies the step:

$$
eg p \wedge(p \vee eg q) \equiv( eg p \wedge p) \vee( eg p \wedge eg q)
$$

  1. De Morgan's law
  2. Absorption law
  3. Distributive law
  4. Associative law
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
Which sequence of laws correctly proves $\mathrm{p} \vee(\mathrm{p} \wedge \mathrm{q}) \vee(\neg \mathrm{p} \wedge \mathrm{r}) \equiv \mathrm{p} \vee \mathrm{r}$ ?

  1. Distributive law, then De Morgan's law, then absorption.
  2. Absorption law on first two terms, then distributive law, then identity law.
  3. De Morgan's law, then absorption, then idempotent law.
  4. Commutative law, then absorption, then identity law.
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
Consider the two formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{F} 1=(\mathrm{p} \wedge \mathrm{q}) \vee(\mathrm{p} \wedge \mathrm{q} \wedge \mathrm{r}) \\
& \mathrm{F} 2=(\mathrm{p} \wedge \mathrm{q} \wedge \mathrm{r}) \vee(\mathrm{p} \wedge \mathrm{q})
\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is correct?

  1. F1 \# F2, their biconditional is a tautology.
  2. $\mathrm{F} 1 \equiv \mathrm{~F} 2$; counterexample: $\mathrm{p}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{q}=\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{r}=\mathrm{T}$ makes them differ.
  3. F1 $\equiv \mathrm{F} 2$; counterexample: $\mathrm{p}=\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{q}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{r}=\mathrm{T}$ makes them differ.
  4. F1 $\equiv \mathrm{F} 2$; counterexample: $\mathrm{p}=\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{q}=\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{r}=\mathrm{F}$ makes them differ.
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
$$
eg \mathrm{I} ightarrow eg \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D} ightarrow \mathrm{~S}, eg \mathrm{P} ightarrow eg \mathrm{D}, eg \mathrm{~S} \vee \mathrm{I}, \mathrm{P} ightarrow \mathrm{C}
$$

Given the five propositions with variables I, S, D, P, C (all assigned TRUE), which of the following assignments make all five propositions simultaneously TRUE? Select all that apply.

  1. $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{S}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{T}$
  2. $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{S}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{T}$
  3. $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{S}=\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{T}$
  4. $I=T, P=F, D=T, S=F, C=F$
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
Consider the statement: "Students cannot skype during the test unless the internet is on."
Let $\mathrm{I}=$ "the internet is on" and $\mathrm{S}=$ "students can skype during the test."
Which propositional formula correctly represents this statement?

  1. $\mathrm{S} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}$
  2. $\mathrm{I} \rightarrow \mathrm{S}$
  3. $\neg \mathrm{I} \rightarrow \mathrm{S}$
  4. $S \wedge \neg I$
question.subject: Mathematical Logic
